situation:
You and your teammate are the director of operations and the director of compliance at LEDGERPOINT RECOVERY GROUP, a debt collection agency that works accounts for regional lenders and medical billing offices. The founder and chief executive officer (judge) leads a company of just over forty collectors and has asked the two of you to settle a purchase the leadership team has argued about for a month.

LEDGERPOINT RECOVERY GROUP is two years old and is spending the last of its first round of funding. The collection platform the agency has used since it opened loses vendor support at the end of the year, and the replacement is the largest purchase the company has ever considered. At the current burn rate, the founder (judge) expects about five months of operating cash once it is paid for.

HARBORWAY SYSTEMS has offered its platform at a steep discount as part of a partnership. Harborway's parent company would route a steady stream of new accounts to LEDGERPOINT RECOVERY GROUP, revenue that would carry the agency into its next funding round. In return, Harborway would write the call scripts used on those accounts, set staffing levels for them, and hold every debtor record on its own servers.

Two things sit against the offer. The agency's contract with its largest client promises that debtor records stay on systems LEDGERPOINT RECOVERY GROUP controls. And the vice president who chaired the vendor review told the two of you last week, in confidence, that they still hold an equity stake in Harborway from a job they left three years ago; the agency's written policy requires anyone with a financial interest in a bidder to step off the review.

The alternatives carry their own costs. Buying the platform the review ranked second, at full price and with no accounts attached, would spend most of the remaining cash and force a hiring freeze the founder (judge) has resisted. Reopening the review and taking the stake to the board would push the purchase past the support cutoff, leave collectors on a failing system through the busiest quarter, and put the vice president's job at risk.

The founder (judge) wants the two of you to explain what makes this decision difficult, to say how the confidence you were given should be handled, and to recommend which purchase the agency will make. You will present in the founder's office. The founder (judge) will greet you and ask to hear your ideas, and after your presentation and questions the founder (judge) will thank you for your work.
